On Oct. 13, a federal jury in the U.S. District Court for the District of Delaware delivered a verdict in favor of Qualcomm. The jury found that Arm breached its Architectural License Agreement and intentionally interfered with the commercialization of Qualcomm’s custom Oryon CPUs. While the jury awarded Qualcomm just $1 on each claim, U.S. District Court Judge Maryellen Noreika must still decide Qualcomm’s requested remedy that could allow it to suspend royalty payments to Arm for up to five years.

“We are gratified that the jury found Arm breached its long-standing Architectural License Agreement (ALA) with Qualcomm, failed to honor its commitments, and intentionally acted to disrupt Qualcomm’s businesses,” said Qualcomm in an official statement. “This outcome is a victory for innovation and competition, and we remain focused on developing and delivering industry-leading semiconductor products including our Oryon CPUs to customers and consumers worldwide.”

The decision is the latest chapter in a four-year legal dispute between two semiconductor companies, ensuring that Qualcomm can proceed with marketing its custom silicon across smartphones, AI personal computers, and automotive platforms without the threat of legal injunctions or compulsory design destruction.

By finding Arm liable for contractual interference, leaking the 2024 license-termination warning letter, and failure to meet support commitments by withholding software patches and chip testing tools, the ruling stabilizes chip availability for major device manufacturers while shifting legal and financial pressure back onto Arm.

“We are pleased with the jury’s decision today finding for Arm on four claims and awarding only one dollar in damages on each of Qualcomm’s other two claims,” Arm said in its official statement. “Despite Qualcomm’s pursuit of this case in an attempt ​to deprive Arm of billions of dollars under our license agreements, the jury’s verdict confirms that Arm operated in ​good faith under its technology license agreement and its award of only $2 confirms the merit of Arm’s arguments in the ‌case.”

Technical distinction driving the conflict

At the center of the conflict between Arm and Qualcomm is a fundamental distinction in how intellectual property is commercialized within the semiconductor industry. Arm operates as an architectural IP licensor rather than a silicon manufacturer. The firm defines the instruction set architecture (ISA), establishing rules governing how software instructions interact with computing hardware.

To monetize this technology, Arm offers two primary licensing structures: technology license agreements (TLA) and architecture license agreements (ALA). Under a TLA, a customer purchases off-the-shelf core designs, such as Arm’s standard Cortex series, and integrates them into a system-on-chip in exchange for licensing fees and per-unit royalties.

Under an ALA, the licensee pays for access to the underlying instruction set architecture, granting the right to engineer custom CPU cores, provided those cores maintain software compatibility. 

Historically, Qualcomm relied on its TLA with Arm. However, as computational demands increased, Qualcomm sought to develop custom cores to improve energy efficiency and performance.

In early 2021, Qualcomm acquired Nuvia, a silicon startup founded by veteran chip architects holding an ALA with Arm tailored to data center processors. Qualcomm integrated Nuvia’s engineering team and designs into its roadmap, leading to the development of the custom Oryon CPU architecture.

Four years of cross-litigation 

The transfer of Nuvia’s design work into Qualcomm’s product portfolio sparked strong resistance from Arm. In March 2022, Arm terminated Nuvia’s license and demanded that Qualcomm destroy all design files derived from Nuvia’s work. Arm asserted that its licensing frameworks prohibited transferring custom designs between distinct corporate entities without explicit consent and renegotiated terms.

When Qualcomm declined to destroy the technology, maintaining that its overarching license covered the development and commercialization of the Oryon cores, Arm filed a lawsuit in Delaware District Court in August 2022. Arm alleged breach of contract and trademark infringement, seeking an injunction to force Qualcomm to halt production of chips containing Nuvia-derived technology.

That initial phase of litigation concluded in legal victories for Qualcomm. In December 2024, a Delaware jury determined that Qualcomm’s custom CPU technology was properly licensed under Qualcomm’s existing ALA and that Qualcomm had not breached the Nuvia contract. On Sept. 30, 2025, the presiding judge issued a final judgment, affirming those jury findings and dismissing Arm’s remaining claims as a matter of law. Arm subsequently filed an appeal with the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit, where the matter remains pending.

While defending against Arm’s claims, Qualcomm launched its own offensive in April 2024, alleging that Arm breached both licensing agreements by failing to deliver technical support, failing to provide reasonable licensing terms, and improperly interfering with Qualcomm’s customer relationships.

The conflict escalated in October 2024 when Arm issued a formal notice threatening to terminate Qualcomm’s overarching ALA entirely—a move that threatened to halt global production of Qualcomm’s Snapdragon processors. Arm withdrew the notice in January 2025, but Qualcomm incorporated the incident into its allegations of bad-faith conduct, leading to the October 2026 trial in Wilmington, Delaware. 

The jury’s decision followed a five-day trial, where jurors evaluated licensing terms and corporate communications between the two companies. After receiving the case on Oct. 9, 2026, the jury returned its verdict on Oct. 13, finding Arm liable for breaching the “Architectural License Agreement” governing how Qualcomm uses Arm’s architecture to build custom processor designs. 

However, the jury sided with Arm on five of the six breach of contract allegations, rejecting Qualcomm’s claims that Arm had violated those specific terms of its technology license agreement.

Financial pressure and win for open standards such as RISC-V

Beyond confirming Qualcomm’s right to commercialize its custom silicon, the October 2026 verdict introduces financial uncertainty for Arm. During the trial, proceedings highlighted a contractual provision that could permit a licensee to suspend royalty payments for five years if Arm commits a material breach.

As of today (Oct. 19), the judge has yet to rule on whether a specific contractual clause—which could allow Qualcomm to entirely cease paying royalties to Arm for a period of five years due to Arm’s material breach of the agreement—is legally enforceable.

If enforced, the financial consequences for Arm could be substantial. Qualcomm represents one of Arm’s largest revenue sources, accounting for approximately 10% of Arm’s total global revenue for fiscal year 2024. A five-year hiatus on royalty collections from Qualcomm would reduce Arm’s cash flows, impacting research funding and market valuation expectations following Arm’s initial public offering in September 2023.

For original equipment manufacturers, the verdict provides operational certainty. Handset makers such as Samsung Electronics, alongside personal computer manufacturers deploying Snapdragon 8 Elite processors and Oryon CPUs, can continue hardware production without risk of supply chain disruptions.

At the same time, the legal battle has altered industry perceptions regarding proprietary architecture licensing. Arm’s willingness to engage in litigation against its premier customer has encouraged semiconductor designers and cloud operators to accelerate investments in open instruction set architectures, such as RISC-V, to mitigate long-term risks.

For now, the Delaware verdict establishes Qualcomm’s legal authority to deploy its custom silicon, reshaping commercial boundaries across the technology sector.

SEMICON West 2026 opened at Moscone Center in San Francisco on a jubilant note: Semiconductors are now a trillion-dollar industry. In his opening keynote, SEMI CEO Ajit Manocha proclaimed the start of happy times and, besides AI, he credited IoT and quantum computing with turning the semiconductor industry into a trillion-dollar behemoth.

The event covered the entire semiconductor manufacturing value chain—lithography, photomasking, wafer inspection, materials, and more—while also offering a detailed look at the AI economy, accelerated EDA, quantum computing, chiplets, and advanced packaging. For instance, Synopsys CEO Sassine Ghazi sat for a fireside chat to explain the role of autonomous AI in chip design.

Zeiss Semiconductor Manufacturing Technology (SMT), which supplies lithography optics and photomask systems for chip fabrication, announced its entry into wafer inspection systems at SEMICON West while showcasing two new products: Zeiss DUNE and Zeiss NLX.

Zeiss DUNE measures wafer topography and can correct it individually, addressing the critical challenge of wafer bow in complex fabrication processes. “Wafer flatness has become a huge issue,” Raghu Nayak, head of U.S. sales for Zeiss SMT, told EE Times. “Zeiss DUNE helps flatten wafers and ensures overlay for next fabrication steps.”

Zeiss NLX, designed for 300-mm wafers, makes internal structures in modern chip packages visible without destroying them. So engineers can inspect connections between stacked dies and detect potential defects early. “These inspection systems will help engineers in wafer-by-wafer adjustments and thus boost precision, process control, and productivity in semiconductor fabrication,” Nayak added.

Next, Mitsubishi Chemical Group (MCG) showcased solutions across its polymers, films, materials, and chemicals portfolios. Fallyn Flaherty-Earp, MCG’s global market director, told EE Times that for polymers, it’s currently readying new materials for semiconductor manufacturing equipment. For films, it’s developing a new biopolymer for PCBs for use in flexible electronics. MCG is also developing new materials for formulated silicon for advanced packaging applications.

At SEMICON West, high-precision vacuum coating equipment supplier Von Ardenne announced it is expanding its semiconductor deposition portfolio to panel-level packaging (PLP). The company’s U.S. CEO, Stephen Strausser, told EE Times that, in advanced packaging, Von Ardenne has a one- to two-year lead in coating and deposition for panel-level glass substrates.

The privately owned German firm’s HiPIMS solution deposits high-aspect-ratio barrier and seed layers in through-glass via (TGV) holes, enabling dense, highly adherent functional-film deposition and improved material performance. This allows semiconductor manufacturers to migrate established deposition processes from 300-mm wafer formats to larger panel form factors for advanced packaging applications, including through-glass vias (TGVs) and redistribution layers (RDL).

Another German firm, Heidenhain, unveiled a new full air-bearing planar platform for the most demanding step‑and‑scan semiconductor applications. The high-precision METIS HP platform includes direct laser writing and high‑resolution optical inspection systems. Heidenhain provides sub-nanometer motion control and position feedback solutions for wafer manufacturing.

SEMICON West wasn’t all about semiconductor manufacturing tech bytes such as wet cleaning, electroplating, and thermal processing. Building a skilled workforce for the new fab buildout was also high on the event’s agenda.

Workforce development has been a key theme, given that the huge front-end and back-end chip fabrication infrastructure is expected to create life-changing careers across different regions of the U.S. Phoenix City Mayor Kate Gallego talked about fab apprenticeship programs in her speech at the event.

Then, there is fab construction specialist ABM, which provides equipment installation, contamination control, and cleanroom services. ABM is gearing up to provide workforce solutions after completing its merger with WGNSTAR, a Dublin, Ireland–founded provider of managed workforce solutions and equipment support services for the semiconductor industry.

Darrell McDaniel, ABM’s VP of Technical Training & Asset Relocation, sees massive fab buildout as a huge opportunity in terms of workforce development and training programs. He pointed to ABM’s Technical Training Center in Boise, Idaho, a recently launched fab skills development program for advanced semiconductor manufacturing with capacity to accommodate about 500 participants annually.

SEMICON West 2026, held on Oct. 13-15, 2026, is a testament to how the semiconductor world has changed and how AI sits right in the center of this transformation. This sense of optimism was everywhere, and industry executives seemed confident the good times are here to stay for now.

As AI workloads redefine the power requirements of modern data centers, power design solutions won a prominent spot at the Open Compute Project (OCP) Global Summit 2026 in San Jose, California. The data center power solutions showcased at the San Jose McEnery Convention Center ranged from 800 V-to-12 V power delivery boards to server power supply units (PSUs) to high-voltage hot-swap controllers.

Navitas Semiconductor displayed a 24-kW, 800 V-to-12 V DC-DC power delivery board it developed with Nvidia. The gallium nitride (GaN)-based 800 V DC power solution for AI data centers supports Nvidia’s MGX server hardware. The board was featured on Nvidia’s AI Factory MGX Wall partner display area at the OCP show floo`r.

The power delivery board, built around the company’s GaNFast power architecture, targets 97% efficiency at full load and a power density exceeding 2,000 W/in³. “The 24-kW solution demonstrates how GaNFast technology can eliminate power-conversion stages, increase efficiency and power density, and bring power closer to the GPU,” said Chris Allexandre, president and CEO of Navitas.

Another board-level power solution for AI data centers displayed at OCP was Infineon’s 27-kW, three-phase power supply unit (PSU). The reference board for AI servers meets the requirements of the OCP Open Rack V3 (ORV3) specification and AI server rack architectures.

The board features a five-level ANPC power factor correction (PFC) topology and a three-level LLC converter, achieving a power density of 116 W/in³ versus the ORV3 minimum requirement of 94 W/in³. The PFC and LLC stages are digitally controlled to respond to demanding AI load transients.

The programmable power control accelerator (PPca), integrated into the PSOC Control C3 microcontroller, supports precise current and voltage regulation with fast dynamic response. In addition to PSOC microcontrollers, the reference board includes 650-V CoolSiC and CoolMOS MOSFETs, EiceDRIVER gate drivers, and XENSIV current sensors.

Another key feature of this reference board for AI servers is an integrated energy buffer that provides 20 milliseconds of hold-up time during short power grid disturbances. This helps smooth the line voltage during rapid GPU load changes, which in turn eliminates the need for a separate capacitor bank unit (CBU).

Power path protection and monitoring

As AI clusters scale from 48 V to higher rack power levels, they increasingly demand reliable hot-swap functionality to maintain uninterrupted system operation. “Future AI data centers require power delivery systems that combine high efficiency, maximum reliability, and comprehensive protection capabilities,” said Magdalene Boebel, senior vice president and business line head of power system ICs at Infineon.

At OCP, Infineon also unveiled a high-voltage hot-swap controller for digital power-path protection and monitoring in AI server power architectures operating at ±400 V and 800 V DC. The XDP8HD40S-1 enables power modules, converters, GPUs, and server subsystems to be connected and disconnected safely while preserving system integrity.

Infineon’s new hot-swap controller is designed for a range of high-voltage applications in AI data centers. Besides 400-V to 800-V single- or dual-side hot-swap implementations, that includes battery backup systems, high-voltage rack and server power delivery, peak shaving, and two-wire 800-V or ±400-V IBC systems.

Texas Instruments also showcased its first 800-V isolated hot-swap controller that delivers in-rush current and power path protection while enabling safe power insertion and fast fault isolation. The LMI800PS, available in a single high-density package, replaces a complex discrete solution that requires five chips.

It is a scalable solution for diverse rack architectures, supporting both ±400-V and 800-V distributions. In AI data center environments, this isolated hot-swap controller prevents a single load failure from disrupting the shared power bus, maximizing data center stability.

Nanosecond-level telemetry

Like Navitas, TI also showcased its 800 V DC power solutions on Nvidia’s MGX AI Factory Ecosystem wall. This included a high-performance 3 gigasamples per second (GSPS) analog-to-digital converter (ADC) that enables 24/7, low-power, event-based remote monitoring at nanosecond resolution.

In data centers, existing monitoring solutions often fail to detect nanosecond-level power-rail glitches, leading to costly, unplanned downtime. The ADC34DSO75 combines ultra-high-speed sampling with advanced on-chip digital signal processing in a small form factor to detect and capture transient fault events in real time.

“As AI workloads drive massive scale, the need for real-time visibility and architectural stability has never been greater,” said Karthik Vasanth, vice president and general manager for TI’s data, converters, and clocks business unit. Power chip vendors like TI are confident that high-performance ADCs and hot-swap controllers featuring high-speed telemetry, advanced power protection, and precision timing capabilities can help data center operators and hyperscalers optimize performance and minimize downtime.

As GPU performance increases and rack densities rise, data center operators face significant challenges regarding power instability and inadequate real-time monitoring. The power solutions showcased at the OCP Global Summit 2026, held Oct. 12–15, aim to close this technology gap by accelerating the deployment of the high-efficiency power systems AI infrastructure requires.

TAIPEI, Taiwan — At EE Times Taiwan’s iTechCon conference, a panel discussion with industry experts and government officials identified talent as a major challenge to Taiwan’s opportunity in AI.

Taiwanese companies are ready to capture more of the design and architectural value, over and above manufacturing, David Wang, senior VP of GPU technologies and engineering at AMD, told EE Times in an exclusive interview after the panel discussion.

“I certainly hope so,” Wang said. “But it will take collaboration between the public and private sectors, because you have to develop people with more systems and software capabilities.”

Talent is a chicken-and-egg situation, since students will continue to choose other fields without intervention, Wang said.  

“[If] you don’t have students, you don’t have talent; you can’t really expand beyond hardware,” he said. “But if you don’t have those industries, you can’t have people develop their talent either. It will be challenging to break that loop unless public and private sectors step in to proactively do something.”

Advanced packaging

Taiwan’s next big opportunity is in advanced packaging as AI expands at rack scale, Wang said, along with networking and silicon photonics. Physical AI is also a huge opportunity since it requires the integration of many disciplines, he added.

“There’s a chip, there’s firmware, there’s software, there’s a system—they may not be complex, but Taiwan is known to collaborate and move fast and be very agile, so that’s how it would fit in well with Taiwan’s ecosystem,” he said.

The AI PC is another huge opportunity, since Taiwan is already the center of the PC ecosystem, Wang said.

“I certainly believe, as we move into physical AI, it’s a pretty good opportunity to replicate [the PC] model,” he said. “However, it needs standards and open standards. Because Taiwan doesn’t have many large companies… The way [smaller companies] can really thrive is to be part of open ecosystems with open standards, so that everybody can participate, everybody can play, and everybody can win.”

Ecosystem and culture

International companies rely on Taiwan’s ecosystems already because of the country’s hardworking and collaborative culture, Wang said.

“You can replicate tools, you can replicate processes, [and] it’s very hard to replicate culture,” he said. “The diligent nature of how they treat work, how they treat customers and customer priorities, I think that is very, very hard to replicate.”

AMD announced $10 billion of investment in Taiwan’s ecosystem earlier this year. This funding will primarily support advanced packaging, Wang said, and advanced substrate capacity, working with AMD’s Taiwanese partners including OSAT ASE, its packaging and test subsidiary SPIL, and packaging company PTI (Powertech).

“We also expanded our planning horizon, since planning for next year is no longer sufficient,” he said. “Our planning horizon is multiple years in advance, so we want to make sure the capacity is enough, because we believe we’re still in an early innings of AI growth.”

Advanced packaging is crucial to AMD’s plans. Wang pointed out that AMD led the transition to chiplets and to 3D stacking.

“In order to do this sort of thing, we have to plan at the architecture level; it can’t be an afterthought,” he said. “We work very closely with our suppliers, particularly TSMC, almost jointly developing those technologies.”

data.title: AI Moves to System-Level Co-Design: How Can Taiwan Capture More Value

As AI workloads shift from model training toward inference, agentic AI, and physical AI, system design is no longer just about maximizing the computing performance of individual chips. Instead, it increasingly requires the co-design of chips, models, software, and system architecture.

At the international roundtable held during the recent 2026 EE Tech Summit (iTechCon 2026), organized by EE Times/EDN Taiwan, experts from government, industry, and research institutions examined how Taiwan could translate its semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, and system integration capabilities into greater value from AI innovation. They also highlighted the need to expand software expertise, cultivate cross-disciplinary talent, and foster a more vibrant startup ecosystem.

Moderating the session, “Taiwan and the Global AI Ecosystem: Building the Next Wave of Innovation,” EE Times senior editor Sally Ward-Foxton framed the discussion around how Taiwan could build on its strong AI hardware supply chain to capture more value as AI evolves from chips and data centers into complete intelligent systems.

AI design moves up to the system level

David Wang, senior VP of GPU Technology and Engineering at AMD, noted that agentic AI depends not only on GPUs for model inference but also on CPUs to execute tasks, orchestrate tools, and manage workflows. This is reshaping the balance of CPU and GPU resources within AI systems. As AI moves further into edge devices, robots, and industrial equipment, power efficiency, low latency, and real-time responsiveness will play an important role in computing architecture design.

Future systems will rely increasingly on heterogeneous computing, allocating CPUs, GPUs, NPUs, and dedicated accelerators according to workload requirements. Wang emphasized that applications differ in their demands for performance, power consumption, latency, reliability, and security, making it impossible for any single architecture to meet every need.

Yung-Hui Li, founding director of the AI Research Center at Hon Hai Research Institute, said AI system design has expanded beyond individual chips to encompass entire racks and even data centers, where compute, memory, interconnects, networking, power delivery, liquid cooling, and software must work together. “A frontier cluster has to behave like one giant computer,” he said.

As workloads move toward inference and agentic AI, bottlenecks increasingly arise beyond computing capacity. Data movement, power delivery, and thermal management can all constrain performance. Li noted that system-level metrics are also evolving, with greater emphasis on performance per watt and tokens generated per dollar rather than floating-point operations per second (FLOPS) alone. As a result, chips, memory, interconnects, and cooling must be co-designed to optimize overall system performance.

Extending hardware strengths to intelligent systems

Taiwan has a comprehensive industrial ecosystem spanning semiconductor manufacturing, advanced packaging, PCBs, power delivery, thermal management, networking, and servers. Li said Taiwan’s advantage lies not only in its chip manufacturing capabilities but also in the close integration of these industries, which enables rapid design integration, validation, and transition to mass production.

Kuo-Hsuan Chen, deputy director general of the Industrial Development Administration (IDA) under Taiwan’s Ministry of Economic Affairs (MOEA), said Taiwan’s long-established industrial supply chains and international partnerships would be difficult for other regions to replicate in a short time. The next step, he said, is to integrate AI models, software and technologies developed by startups into existing industry collaborations to develop intelligent systems for real-world applications.

Wang sees an opportunity for AMD and its Taiwanese partners to build an open robotics ecosystem modeled on the AI PC ecosystem experience, enabling companies across the industry to participate. Taiwan’s strengths in the semiconductor supply chain, advanced packaging, and system integration could help accelerate the development of edge AI and physical AI, he said.

AMD is also expanding its collaboration with Taiwan’s industrial ecosystem. In May 2026, AMD announced plans to invest more than $10 billion in Taiwan’s ecosystem to expand strategic partnerships and scale advanced packaging capabilities for AI infrastructure. The company is also working with Taiwanese partners through the MOEA’s A+ Global R&D and Innovation Partnership Program on research in servers, data centers, silicon photonics, advanced packaging, and AI.

Co-designing chips, models, and software

Yung-Long Lin, founder, chairman, and CEO of Neuchips, noted that many Taiwanese IC design companies historically emerged as spinoffs from established businesses or found niche opportunities within manufacturing and IT supply chains. For Taiwan to build AI chip companies with global influence, he said, the industry must move beyond these traditional models and participate more actively in international standards development and ecosystem building.

Lin emphasized that chips alone cannot deliver a competitive advantage. Models, software, circuits, and chip architectures must be optimized together. Performance can be improved incrementally through advances in computer architecture, linear algebra, and algorithms. Even gains of just 1% or 2% at a time can add up to a meaningful advantage. Such co-design, he stressed, must begin early in the development process. Designers cannot simply finish a chip and then hand it over to software engineers to “clean it up.”

Li added that memory bandwidth, interconnects, and power constraints all influence model architecture and inference strategies. Techniques such as low-precision computing and sparsity must be paired with models that can fully exploit their benefits. For edge AI and robotics, developers must also build efficient models that operate within tight power and memory budgets, while using compilers and runtime environments to orchestrate different accelerators.

Taiwanese startups face challenges including a lack of early customers, real-world deployment data, and long-term funding. Chen said corporate venture capital (CVC), joint R&D, and testing environments could help startups gain access to capital, technology, real-world application scenarios, and customer networks. Li added that large companies could serve as early customers for startups and research institutions by providing real workflows, data, and testing environments. Investors, meanwhile, could offer greater support for software and platform companies.

Reflecting on Taiwan’s startup environment, Lin described the experience as follows: “[Launching] startups is hard, but it’s helpful, and it’s fun.” Large technology companies can cultivate talent and provide valuable technical and business experience, equipping people who may eventually launch their own ventures or collaborate with startups. However, Taiwanese society still tends to favor stable employment, and graduates and their families may be reluctant to embrace the risks of entrepreneurship. Citing the recent debate over Taiwan’s NT$10,000 (~$309) universal cash handout, Lin urged Taiwan to consider how its resources and collective efforts could better support the industry’s long-term development.

Physical AI demands real-time performance and cross-disciplinary talent

As AI moves into robots, factories, and smart devices, systems must integrate multimodal sensor inputs—including camera, depth, force, and tactile data—and make decisions in real time within power and thermal constraints. Li explained that physical AI requires a different computing architecture from that used in data centers. Large-scale model training and world-model learning can take place in the cloud, but perception and control must run in real time at the edge. Control loops may require responses within milliseconds, making reliance on round-trip network communication impractical.

An incorrect answer from a chatbot may cause little more than inconvenience, Li said, but a malfunctioning robot on a factory floor could damage equipment or injure people. Safety, reliability, verification, and redundancy are therefore essential. Because real-world environments do not provide the large volumes of data needed for training, developers must combine simulation environments, digital twins, synthetic data, and world models to narrow the gap between simulation and real-world deployment. Foxconn’s factories can provide environments for field testing and data collection, helping developers validate physical AI systems, he added.

On the talent front, Wang said the global AI industry faces a shortage of skilled professionals, particularly those who can work across traditional disciplinary boundaries and think at the system level. Engineers must also learn to use AI tools effectively, coordinate multiple agents to accomplish tasks, and even leverage AI to develop better AI systems.

Lin cautioned that even when AI can help write code, engineers still need a solid foundation in computer science to assess code quality and identify problems. Taiwan built its hardware advantage through engineering education, he said, and must now extend that strength to software and systems education. It must also provide upskilling opportunities for working professionals and people from other disciplines.

Chen said that over the next five years, Taiwanese companies should become better at integrating new technologies and startup approaches into their R&D processes, while involving talent with AI software and data expertise in decision-making.

Li concluded with a benchmark for determining whether Taiwan has truly become a center of AI innovation: “The world looks to Taiwan for ideas and products, not just manufacturing.”

data.title: Japan Offers GlobalFoundries $21B for U.S. Fab Expansion

Japan has offered up to $21 billion to GlobalFoundries to expand its existing U.S. semiconductor complex in an unprecedented public-private partnership between the two nations and the fifth-largest chip foundry by sales. Analysts voiced concerns that the company may be too dependent on government support.

Under the agreement, GlobalFoundries will build and run two new chip fabs at its existing Malta, New York, site under a U.S.-Japan trade and investment agreement led by the administration of U.S. President Donald Trump, who has pledged to return chipmaking to the U.S.

The initiative will accelerate U.S. chip production, strengthen critical supply chains, and support growing AI demand, the company said in an Oct. 14 press release. After the two fabs enter production, U.S. capacity will increase by about 10%, GlobalFoundries CEO Tim Breen said on a webcast.

The investment also reduces Japan’s geographic concentration risk, Breen said. GlobalFoundries hailed the new investment model, expecting to achieve profit per silicon wafer similar to current margins without incurring associated fixed costs in the tens of billions of dollars, the company said.

Japan is a major chipmaking nation, yet most of its production remains at home. The global chip industry, meanwhile, has evolved beyond borders.

“This is a bold new initiative for semiconductor manufacturing, bringing together the U.S. and Japan with GF’s differentiated technology and decades of manufacturing expertise to accelerate trusted capacity in New York,” Breen noted.

Existing GlobalFoundries customers, including Apple, Renesas, General Motors, and Cirrus Logic, gave their endorsement to the plan. GlobalFoundries has also been a trusted supplier of chips to the U.S. military.

“We are planning around GF’s new capacity in New York as an extension of Renesas’s own production footprint, trusted U.S.-based manufacturing backed by a strong U.S.-Japan partnership,” Renesas CEO Hidetoshi Shibata said in the release. “These capabilities are essential as we deliver advanced solutions, with demand for electrification, connectivity, AI, and data center applications accelerating worldwide.”

“We’ve partnered with GlobalFoundries to produce essential chips for Apple products right here in the U.S., as part of our $600 billion commitment to American investment,” said Sabih Khan, Apple’s COO, in the release.

“GM is making strategic investments in autonomy and centralized computing to power the next generation of software-defined vehicles and deliver customer-focused technologies at scale, including widespread deployment of AI across our vehicles and breakthrough capabilities,” GM president Mark Reuss said. “GM and GF established the first direct automaker-to-foundry supply agreement, and expanding domestically owned and operated fab capacity in upstate New York marks a decisive step forward for American manufacturing.”

The first fab, backed by a $10 billion investment, is scheduled to begin production in 2029. The first fab will add about 900,000 300-mm wafers to annual U.S. capacity when fully loaded. The second facility will reach the same target.

U.S. investment

Under the Trump administration, the U.S. government has pursued partnerships with the semiconductor industry.

The U.S. Department of Commerce (DoC) said it will take a 4% equity stake in GlobalFoundries, enabling the American public to share in GlobalFoundries’ growth. The U.S. government more than a year ago took a 10% equity stake in GlobalFoundries’ rival Intel. The U.S. recently awarded $1 billion in R&D funding to Anderon, IBM’s new quantum chip foundry, in New York.

GlobalFoundries has agreed with the DoC to change an existing CHIPS Act award to reallocate $955 million to the company to boost earlier investments in silicon photonics, silicon-germanium (SiGe), and advanced packaging at facilities in Malta and Burlington, Vermont.

Analysts expressed concern that the company may be relying too heavily on government support.

“The new investments from Japan along with the reallocation of funds to silicon photonics and related technologies will strengthen GF’s ability to serve customers that prefer U.S.-based manufacturing capacity,” BNP Paribas Equity Research senior analyst Karl Ackerman said in a report provided to EE Times. “The U.S. government’s decision to take this significant equity stake is a meaningful positive for GF, effectively positioning the company as a government-backed strategic supplier. However, we think today’s news also underscores the extent to which GF’s long-term growth prospects lean on government intervention rather than free-market competitiveness.”

GlobalFoundries-TSMC partnership

GlobalFoundries has been one of the first foundries to enter the silicon photonics business.

On Oct. 8, GlobalFoundries announced an agreement with TSMC for a U.S.-based supply of silicon interposers for TSMC’s CoWoS advanced packaging that has been a production bottleneck, according to analysts surveyed by EE Times. Under the agreement, GlobalFoundries will add capacity at its New York facility, supporting growing AI demand.

Production is slated for the first half of 2028. The agreement has an initial term of five years and provides for future expansion.

TSMC declined to comment, citing a quiet period leading up to the company’s quarterly earnings announcement today.

TSMC reported record sales and profit for the third quarter of 2026. The world’s top chip foundry said it has been investing carefully in capacity expansion, projected to be somewhere between $60 billion and $64 billion this year.

Even so, TSMC CEO C.C. Wei said on an earnings call with analysts today that the company has “no intention of leaving food on the table for others” in the foundry business. Wei added that the company has been evaluating Texas after expansion of its first “gigafab” in Phoenix, Arizona.

data.title: Small Volumes, Big Impact: Europe’s Hidden Role in Advanced Chipmaking
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

At the Fraunhofer Institute for Silicon Technology (ISIT) in northern Germany, engineers manufacture a very small number of specialized semiconductor chips. By the standards of an industry accustomed to producing millions of chips, the output is negligible. Yet these components help operate equipment used by Intel and TSMC to manufacture some of the world’s most advanced semiconductors.

The customer is IMS Nanofabrication, an Austrian company that builds multibeam electron-beam systems for rapidly writing photomasks used in EUV lithography at technology nodes of 5 nm and below. Fraunhofer supplies a critical component of those machines: a chip containing hundreds of thousands of individually controlled structures that allow each electron beam to be controlled independently.

The relationship illustrates a little-recognized part of the semiconductor value chain. While governments compete to attract advanced fabs, Europe already supplies specialized technologies on which those fabs depend.

“We’re operating in a niche that conventional semiconductor foundries aren’t really set up to serve,” Fabian Lofink, deputy director of Fraunhofer ISIT, told EE Times. “The volumes are very small. The technology is extremely complex. At these production levels, you can’t rely on statistical process control the way high-volume fabs do, so engineers need to be closely involved in manufacturing every day. “

From a thousand beams to hundreds of thousands

The collaboration began in 2005 through publicly funded research. As semiconductor features shrank, the corresponding lithography masks required increasingly dense patterns, driving up electron-beam writing times. Multibeam technology offered a solution by allowing many electron beams to write in parallel.

“As feature sizes shrink, you need to write far more data onto the mask,” Lofink explained. “With a conventional single-beam writer, that directly translates into longer write times. The idea behind multibeam technology was to parallelize the process, enabling high-throughput mask writing even for the most advanced technology nodes.”

The first demonstrator measured one square millimeter and contained 1,000 cells. By 2012, Fraunhofer and partners had developed a chip with approximately 262,000 individually controlled cells.

Fraunhofer does not manufacture the underlying CMOS circuitry. Instead, the chips are fabricated using advanced CMOS technology with feature sizes below 50 nm to achieve the data rates required for multibeam operation. Fraunhofer then adds the structures that enable individual electron beams to be controlled.

This post-CMOS processing requires electroplated gold electrodes, chosen for their high conductivity and ability to support rapid beam control.

“Gold is normally something you don’t want anywhere near a CMOS fabrication line because of contamination,” Lofink said. “But in our application, even the slightest charging effects can distort the electron beam trajectories. Gold provides both the excellent conductivity needed for high-speed beam control and a reliable path for dissipating charge. Our expertise is in combining these materials after the CMOS process without damaging the electronics.”

Some gold structures approach 50 micrometers in height, far beyond conventional planar semiconductor dimensions.

Around 2015, IMS began selling mask-writing systems incorporating the second-generation TROM2 chip to produce photomasks for the 7-nm technology nodes. Fraunhofer continues to manufacture that component.

Too specialized for conventional foundries

The biggest question is: Why does IMS continue to buy from a research organization rather than a commercial foundry?

“Conventional foundries are looking for business cases involving at least 10,000 wafers a year,” Lofink said. “We’re operating at volumes roughly two orders of magnitude below that threshold.  That’s a completely different manufacturing environment.”

The Fraunhofer process also involves approximately 15 lithography levels beyond the CMOS fabrication, specialized materials, and demanding quality requirements.

“High complexity, low volume—that’s our niche,” Lofink said. “You cannot manufacture these products simply by putting operators in front of machines and asking them to push buttons. You need engineers working with the process every day to maintain the required quality.”

High-volume manufacturers use extensive production data to identify variations and stabilize processes. Very small production runs provide fewer opportunities to accumulate such data, increasing the importance of direct engineering supervision.

Fraunhofer also combines experimental research with the ability to supply components reliably. “What differentiates us from a university is that we can take research into an industrial environment,” Lofink said. “We can deliver the same quality repeatedly, and we can deliver it when the customer needs it.”

A small supplier with strong influence

The arrangement has created a supply chain dependency. Fraunhofer remains the key source of TROM2, and transferring production elsewhere would require substantial development.

“If our production stopped, IMS would have a serious problem,” Lofink said. “They have some stock, of course, but you cannot simply move this technology to another supplier. Developing the process takes years.”

For the latest version, TROM3, which is the third generation of the chip, IMS has expanded its manufacturing ecosystem. According to Lofink, it contains approximately 590,000 control cells and supports higher data rates.

The importance of the chips extends far beyond their production volume. IMS’s systems write masks for advanced semiconductor manufacturing, including EUV processes. Lofink identifies Intel and TSMC as major users.

The chips themselves use comparatively mature CMOS technology. “The CMOS in our chip might use a 100-nm or 50-nm process, but the equipment it goes into is used to make masks for 5-nm or 2-nm technology,” Lofink explained.

Extending the model across Europe

For Dirk Schumann, director of the APECS pilot line at the Research Fab Microelectronics Germany (FMD), the IMS relationship illustrates an industrial model that Europe can expand. “If you compare the price of the components we supply with the industrial business they enable, the leverage can be a factor of 50 to 100,” he told EE Times.

The estimate reflects his assessment of the potential downstream value of specialized components, rather than a measured return for the IMS collaboration. Schumann distinguished between the requirements of high-volume chipmakers and those of equipment manufacturers, medical technology companies, and other specialized customers.

“If you’re talking about a company such as Intel or TSMC, they may come to a pilot line for early development, but once they move toward volume manufacturing, they need a different infrastructure,” he said. “For an equipment manufacturer, it’s different. They may need only a limited number of very advanced components, and we can continue supplying those components.”

FMD operates through 13 Fraunhofer institutes and two Leibniz institutes, offering capabilities from technology development through prototyping and small-volume manufacturing. “Our customers don’t need to own the entire infrastructure by themselves,” Schumann said. “We can take a company from an initial idea through technology development, design, prototyping, and even small-volume manufacturing.”

The IMS collaboration predates APECS by many years. Although it didn’t create that relationship, APECS seeks to extend the underlying model through additional capabilities and European partners. Its distributed network aims to give industrial customers access to specialized facilities through a single point of contact, spanning materials, semiconductor processing, and advanced packaging.

Schumann emphasized that developing new technologies is only part of Fraunhofer’s mission. “The real difference comes when we can turn those technologies into industrial value by supplying components that companies can use in their products,” he said.

From technical capability to industrial delivery

APECS is developing 11 demonstrators across four technology areas: high-performance computing, sensors, optical technologies, and RF applications. Beyond proving the technologies themselves, the projects are testing whether geographically dispersed research facilities can operate as a coordinated industrial supplier.

“Technically, moving wafers or chiplets between different institutes isn’t necessarily the biggest challenge,” Schumann said. “The interesting part is making the whole system work as a business: preparing quotations, planning production, coordinating the different facilities, and delivering what the customer has ordered.”

Industrial interest is emerging. According to Schumann, four demonstrators have attracted customers seeking evaluation hardware. “The total number of project requests at APECS, primarily from industrial customers, has already exceeded 200,” he said. How many will lead to sustained commercial production, and when, remains uncertain.

The Fraunhofer–IMS relationship demonstrates what that transition requires: not simply manufacturing a specialized component, but delivering it consistently, reliably, and on schedule. APECS aims to replicate that model across a much larger European network.

Europe’s contribution to advanced chipmaking cannot be measured by production volume alone. Fraunhofer manufactures the specialized chips it supplies to IMS in tiny quantities, yet they play a critical role in equipment used by some of the world’s largest semiconductor manufacturers.

data.title: Benchmark Electronics’ Thailand Operations Focus on High-Mix Manufacturing
data.description:

As electronics manufacturing services (EMS) providers across Southeast Asia race to capture supply chain diversification opportunities, Benchmark Electronics’ Thailand operations focus on engineering, complex manufacturing, and value-added services rather than production scale alone.

For Benchmark Electronics, Thailand is more than a production base. It has become a strategic engineering and manufacturing hub capable of supporting highly regulated industries, advanced communications, medical devices, aerospace, industrial automation, and emerging optical technologies.

“Our business has always been high-mix, low-volume manufacturing,” said Ken Hendrickson, VP Quality/Engineering, Asia, Benchmark Electronics, during a media briefing and facility tour in Ayutthaya. “That’s what we’ve grown up on, and it’s still what we do today.”

Building on Thailand’s manufacturing ecosystem

Benchmark Electronics is a $2.7 billion global EMS provider with operations spanning design engineering, supply chain management, manufacturing, testing, and aftermarket services. Globally, the company operates 24 locations across eight countries, supported by approximately 12,000 employees and eight design centers.

Thailand hosts two of its largest manufacturing sites—in Ayutthaya and Nakhon Ratchasima—employing roughly 3,500 people. Together, the facilities support industries requiring stringent quality, traceability, and engineering expertise, including medical electronics, RF communications, satellite systems, industrial controls, and advanced computing.

The company’s confidence in Thailand extends beyond its manufacturing footprint.

Executives pointed to the country’s mature industrial infrastructure, reliable utilities, experienced workforce, and investment incentives offered by Thailand’s Board of Investment (BOI) as key reasons for continued expansion.

“The infrastructure here in Thailand is very good—from industrial parks, power supply, water supply, and people,” said Aldo Coley, VP and general manager, Thailand Operations. “We also very much enjoy the benefits and incentives we receive through BOI promotions, whether for new equipment investments or tax incentives.”

Engineering talent as a competitive advantage

Benchmark Electronics believes Thailand’s greatest competitive advantage remains its engineering talent.

Rather than relying solely on experienced hires, the company combines recruitment with long-term workforce development through internal training, certification programs, university collaborations, and internship initiatives.

“We recruit for skills,” said Hendrickson. “When we’re looking for RF people or engineers with microelectronics experience, many of our competitors are also here. That means there’s already an experienced labor pool we can draw from.”

The company supplements external hiring with continuous internal development.

“We have extensive training programs, annual certification and recertification, and partnerships with universities,” Coley said. “We also run internship programs. There are many ways we can reach out and develop talent.”

That investment appears to be paying off.

Benchmark Electronics reports annual employee turnover below 1%, while production operators average between 10 and 12 years of tenure—an important advantage when manufacturing highly regulated products requiring consistent process discipline.

High-mix manufacturing expertise

While many EMS providers pursue high-volume consumer electronics, Benchmark Electronics said it deliberately focuses on complex products with smaller production volumes.

The Ayutthaya facility alone performs approximately 1,000 manufacturing line changeovers every month.

“Every three or four hours, we’re changing over a production line,” Hendrickson said.

Managing that level of manufacturing flexibility requires sophisticated planning, inventory management, supplier coordination, and engineering support—areas Benchmark Electronics considers core competencies.

“I don’t know another EMS that does this high-mix, low-volume work with so many customers,” Hendrickson said. “That’s been our business throughout the company’s history.”

The company manufactures products ranging from FDA-regulated medical devices and RF systems operating up to 86 GHz to satellite communications equipment, industrial control systems, HDTV broadcast equipment, GNSS positioning systems, and increasingly sophisticated digital LiDAR platforms.

Beyond contract manufacturing

Benchmark Electronics argued that modern EMS competition increasingly depends on engineering services rather than manufacturing equipment alone.

“For the most part, any EMS can build a PCBA,” Hendrickson said. “We all have similar equipment and systems.”

Instead, Benchmark Electronics invests in capabilities customers increasingly value, including test development, failure analysis, process engineering, automation development, microelectronics packaging, design-for-manufacturability, and design-for-test, among others.

In fact, its Regional Technology Center in Thailand provides in-house materials analysis, process validation, troubleshooting, and failure analysis, enabling engineers to diagnose production issues without relying entirely on component suppliers.

“When there’s a production issue, the faster you can identify the root cause, the faster you recover,” Hendrickson said.

Rather than waiting for suppliers to investigate defective components, Benchmark performs much of the diagnosis internally, reducing production delays and improving customer responsiveness.

Automation supporting—not replacing—people

Automation has also become a growing focus.

Recognizing changing manufacturing requirements several years ago, Benchmark Electronics established a dedicated automation engineering team at its Korat facility.

“We started about five or six years ago,” Hendrickson noted. “We didn’t have an automation team then, but we knew we’d need those capabilities.”

Today, the group consists of 17 engineers developing robotics, custom automation systems, and manufacturing equipment for Benchmark Electronics’ operations across Thailand and other global sites.

Rather than replacing workers, the company views automation as another engineering competency supporting increasingly complex manufacturing.

Benefiting from ASEAN’s supply chain shift

Benchmark Electronics also sees Thailand benefiting from broader geopolitical shifts reshaping global electronics supply chains.

As manufacturers diversify beyond China, Southeast Asia has become an increasingly important production region.

“Many international companies are de-risking from China,” Coley said. “They’re looking at alternatives such as Vietnam, the Philippines, Malaysia—and we’re right in the middle of all that.”

The company’s regional presence enables it to leverage ASEAN trade agreements while working with suppliers across neighboring countries to strengthen supply chain resilience and improve export competitiveness for customers serving markets including India, Europe, China, and the U.S.

Organic growth remains the priority

Although Thailand has become a major manufacturing hub for electric vehicles (EVs), Benchmark Electronics is not currently pursuing large-scale EV manufacturing opportunities.

Instead, the company continues to focus on its traditional strengths while expanding into optical products, including LiDAR systems and advanced sensing technologies.

Growth is expected to come primarily through existing customer expansion and new program wins.

“We’re growing organically,” Coley said. “Some new customers have had very good success with us and are moving additional business from other contract manufacturers into Thailand.”

That growth is already visible inside the Ayutthaya campus, where previously unused factory space is now filled with new production programs.

As supply chains continue evolving, Benchmark Electronics is confident that engineering capability, not just manufacturing capacity, will determine which EMS providers emerge as long-term partners for increasingly complex electronics products.

data.title: Beyond Lithography: 3D Scaling Puts New Demands on Materials
data.description:
//php echo do_shortcode('[responsivevoice_button voice="US English Male" buttontext="Listen to Post"]') ?>

For decades, semiconductor scaling has been described largely in terms of shrinking dimensions. But as logic and memory structures increasingly extend vertically as well as laterally, printing smaller features is only part of the manufacturing challenge.

“The challenge rotates now,” Stephen Sopko, semiconductor and deep-tech practice lead at HyperFRAME Research, told EE Times. Instead of thinking primarily about patterning structures from above, manufacturers increasingly have to grow, etch, and fill them in three dimensions, controlling materials on surfaces that may be buried within increasingly complex devices.

Lithography remains essential. Sopko described it as “setting the pitch and the critical dimension.” But once those increasingly small dimensions have been defined, deposition, etch, and materials engineering play growing roles in determining whether the resulting structures can actually be manufactured at scale.

That transition is creating opportunities for semiconductor equipment companies to rethink materials that have performed relatively straightforward jobs for decades.

ASM International is targeting one of those opportunities with Flowable Carbon, its plasma-enhanced chemical vapor deposition (PECVD) technology designed to fill complex 3D structures while creating a planar surface. The company said the technology can, in some process flows, eliminate subsequent chemical mechanical planarization (CMP) and etch-back steps.

Carbon and the challenges of 3D scaling

Carbon films have been used in semiconductor manufacturing for more than two decades, including as hard masks during patterning. But the structures those films must accommodate are changing.

“In the past four or five years, a lot of logic foundry companies have started working on gate-all-around devices,” Tyler Sample, VP and head of ASM’s PECVD product unit, told EE Times. “Those devices, of course, are 3D in nature.”

3D NAND has confronted three-dimensional manufacturing challenges for considerably longer. Now logic is joining it, while hybrid bonding and chiplet integration introduce additional 3D structures. Sample expects DRAM eventually to move further into the third dimension as well.

The problem isn’t simply that structures are getting taller. Traditional PECVD carbon can be deposited conformally over a structure, but as geometries become more complex, Sample said manufacturers can encounter variations in film quality and uniformity along the depth of a feature. Depending on the geometry, voids or seams can also form.

Gate-all-around transistors illustrate the changing problem. Rather than simply coating a surface, materials may need to surround nanosheets and fill spaces laterally as well as vertically.

“You pattern it, you get the critical dimensions, but now they’re so small,” Sample said. “Can you fill in three directions at the same time while being planar once you fill the feature?”

ASM’s answer is to change the behavior of the carbon itself. “When we say flowable, it is truly flowable,” Sample said.

The deposition and subsequent treatments allow the material to reflow into structures rather than relying solely on conventional conformal deposition. Sample said the approach can accommodate geometries ranging from gate-all-around structures to much larger openings encountered in memory and other applications. “What really makes this unique is the chemistry and the material itself,” he said.

ASM is drawing on its experience developing materials for atomic layer deposition (ALD) as it expands its PECVD business. Sample said research teams in Belgium and Finland work to identify materials that address problems raised by customers. ASM then develops the equipment and processes needed to use those materials in semiconductor manufacturing.

Flowable Carbon is also designed to self-planarize. ASM deposits enough material to create an overburden above the underlying features. During subsequent processing, the material moves toward a flat upper surface.

That property potentially eliminates another problem created by increasingly complicated structures: what to do after filling them.

Fewer steps, fewer opportunities for defects

In a conventional process, deposited material that fails to meet planarization requirements may require CMP to create the flat surface needed for subsequent processing. Sample said CMP involving carbon-based materials can itself be challenging.

Because ASM’s carbon self-planarizes, some process flows can eliminate that CMP step. ASM’s equipment can also perform an in-situ etch-back, potentially eliminating a separate etch step.

“You can eliminate a CMP step and an etch step,” Sample said, adding that removing steps becomes increasingly valuable as semiconductor manufacturing grows more complicated.

Sopko pointed to the complexity of advanced semiconductor manufacturing, where producing a single chip can involve up to 1,000 process steps, each requiring precise control. Every additional process introduced to improve device performance brings another risk of compromising throughput or yield.

“Every time we increase the complexity, it increases the challenges to making it at scale,” he said. “Yield is everything for a semiconductor company.”

Sample made much the same point from an equipment supplier’s perspective. Eliminating a process step can remove defects associated with the equipment performing that step while also reducing cost. But he sees yield and output as the larger prize. “Given today’s age of AI, output and yield are king,” he said.

ASM initially expects Flowable Carbon to have its greatest impact in gate-all-around devices, but Sample said memory manufacturers are also evaluating the technology.

As 3D NAND continues scaling vertically, the aspect ratios manufacturers must process become increasingly extreme. Sample said ASM has demonstrated its material in gate-all-around-type structures with aspect ratios of roughly 5:1 to 10:1 and in 3D NAND structures reaching around 200:1. The company has also worked with much larger features associated with packaging.

The material has been tested at temperatures ranging from about 200°C to close to 900°C, according to Sample, allowing ASM to address different thermal requirements in logic and memory manufacturing.

Sample expects future 3D DRAM architectures to create additional demand for fill technologies, potentially within five to seven years.

Importantly, Flowable Carbon is not merely a research demonstration. Sample said it is already in high-volume production, and ASM is engaged with all major chipmakers. The development program began roughly six or seven years ago, as the company anticipated emerging requirements in logic and memory.

Scaling beyond lithography

The growing importance of materials does not diminish the importance of lithography. High-NA EUV, Sample said, is needed to achieve the critical dimensions required by future devices. But defining those dimensions creates the next set of problems: depositing materials uniformly around increasingly complicated structures, filling them without seams or voids, etching them accurately, and maintaining planar surfaces.

Sopko sees the transition from FinFETs to nanosheets as a clear example. With FinFETs, fin width was a critical dimension. Nanosheet structures introduce sheet thickness and alternating layers of materials such as silicon and silicon germanium, putting greater emphasis on materials science.

For Sopko, meeting the power, thermal, and performance requirements of increasingly three-dimensional structures will require more materials breakthroughs—and faster development of them.

The transition also spreads the challenge further across the semiconductor equipment value chain. Sopko pointed to metrology as an example. Voids and other defects can become buried inside complex structures, making them increasingly difficult to detect without destroying the wafer. “If you can’t see a void, you can’t fix it,” he said.

For ASM, those changes create an opportunity to expand beyond the areas where it has traditionally been strongest. The company is best known for atomic layer deposition and epitaxy. Sample said ASM is now taking the materials discovery expertise developed in those businesses and applying it to PECVD.

ASM faces competition from established PECVD suppliers, notably Applied Materials and Lam Research. Sample acknowledged that one of ASM’s challenges is persuading customers accustomed to thinking of the company as an ALD supplier to consider it for PECVD.

“We’re trying to carve out our part of that market and actually grow the PECVD market with this technology,” Sample said.

Flowable Carbon gives ASM an entry point based on materials innovation rather than simply another deposition tool. Its presence in high-volume production suggests customers are already willing to test that proposition.

The opportunity could broaden as devices become still more three-dimensional. Sample points beyond GAA toward complementary FET, or CFET, architectures, which stack n-type and p-type devices vertically and would impose additional demands on deposition and materials. Advanced packaging is also beginning to require processes and materials that resemble those traditionally associated with front-end wafer manufacturing.

The result is not a semiconductor roadmap that moves beyond lithography, but one in which lithography is increasingly intertwined with materials, deposition, etch, planarization, and metrology.

Printing smaller features remains fundamental. But as those features extend further into the third dimension, the ability to build around, between, and inside them will increasingly determine whether continued scaling can be manufactured at acceptable yield.

BARCELONA, Spain — In Spain, a new alliance between a state-backed investment entity, an industrial defense giant, and a deep-tech startup aims to offer a blueprint for building domestic alternatives in strategic computing infrastructure.

Qilimanjaro Quantum Tech, a Barcelona-based full-stack quantum computing startup, has completed a €19.6 million (~$21.3 million) first close of its Series A financing round. Spanish defense and technology multinational Indra Group led the round, investing €10 million (~$11.2 million) through its AI subsidiary, IndraMind.     

The partnership is twofold: IndraMind acts as an investor and as a technology partner to develop quantum solutions for AI and cybersecurity, which are essential to protect areas of national and European interest.

The Spanish Society for Technological Transformation (SETT), a public fund under Spain’s Ministry for Digital Transformation and Public Administration, also renewed its backing with a €9.6 million (~$10.5 million) injection. This deal is part of a broader European effort to combine public funding with established industry partners to protect key intellectual property.     

Qilimanjaro intends to use the funds to advance the development of quantum computing solutions and integrate them with high-performance classical computing in multimodal systems.

Hybrid capital model for deep tech

For deep-tech founders, securing multi-million-euro investments means managing technical development while continuously raising capital. “You always have the double job of working on the technological side and, on the other hand, looking for the money for it,” Qilimanjaro CEO Marta Estarellas told EE Times in an interview. Speaking about the initial Series A tranche, Estarellas emphasized that the capital raise remains an active process: “We were in this process of capital raising, and we still are. This is not a final closing of the round, simply the first entry of funds.”

Indra’s and SETT’s entry brought together two distinct financial levers. SETT channeled its contribution through instruments such as the PERTE Chip facility, designed to strengthen Spain’s microelectronics and semiconductor ecosystem under NextGenerationEU recovery funds.

Estarellas noted that the deal moved unusually fast because of institutional deadlines and corporate execution. “Everything came accelerated because SETT had to move a series of funds within specific dates, and Indra demonstrated diligence and agility to move this operation that was completely amazing,” she said.

She observed that Indra is undergoing a major internal restructuring to guarantee technological sovereignty in strategic industries. In an official statement, Estarellas summarized the rationale behind the partnership: “SETT’s renewed commitment and Indra’s entry bring together sovereign capital and industrial capital to protect, but also accelerate, national technological autonomy.”

From flood management to AI

This partnership marks a change in how defense companies work with quantum hardware specialists. “I had a vision of Indra as a very typical defense company, but what we have seen is that it is not like that,” Estarellas told EE Times. She highlighted Indra’s work in emergency management, space, and AI.

Among the immediate joint opportunities is emergency response—a pressing priority following severe floods in Spain. “The convergence of quantum computing along with quantum tech with space, and something that interests them enormously—and us as well—is the convergence between quantum computing and artificial intelligence,” Estarellas said.

Indra Group, with €5.46 billion (~$6.1 billion) in revenue in 2025 and operations in over 140 countries, gives Qilimanjaro access to markets such as transportation, logistics, and network optimization. Through IndraMind, Indra Group said it aims to integrate quantum AI across different projects, combining synthetic data, flexible architectures, and realistic environments.

For Qilimanjaro, the partnership with an established company provides access to distribution channels and markets that could help bring its technology to market. “It is very transversal, and for us it works well because it is like going with a big cousin who helps you, opens doors, introduces you to new markets, and ultimately helps you scale and grow,” Estarellas said.

Scaling hardware for the global race

Founded in Barcelona in 2019, Qilimanjaro employs 80 workers from over 22 nationalities and has deployed eight quantum systems. The company builds full-stack quantum platforms—integrating proprietary chips, control electronics, cryogenics, and software based on superconducting fluxonium qubits.

Three of its systems operate directly within the Barcelona Supercomputing Center (BSC). One of them is Europe’s first analog quantum computer integrated into a high-performance supercomputing hub.

Qilimanjaro initially focused on making analog quantum chips that can be used right away for simulation and optimization and require less error correction. Now, the company is expanding its technology approach by starting to develop digital quantum chips. “We are making a much more ambitious technological roadmap, and once we have it completely aligned, it puts us in a global race,” Estarellas told EE Times. “We are going a bit beyond what was purely analog quantum computing and starting to enter the digital modality, because our hardware is giving us very good results.”

By anchoring manufacturing and design capabilities in Barcelona, the alliance aims to ensure that European quantum research translates into long-term commercial value, rather than intellectual property that is developed or owned elsewhere. As Estarellas put it: “Together, we are joining forces to bring quantum computing closer to strategic industrial sectors and to ensure that the quantum technology built in Spain continues to grow in Spain.”

Singapore-based solid-state transformer (SST) startup Amperesand aims to help AI data centers smooth the spikes in their electrical demand that can stress power grids.

“When a glitch happens, we don’t just kick off the grid; we actually power the AI load with a battery,” Amperesand CEO Brian Dow told EE Times. “We also can pull power to keep the rate of change in the medium voltage under control.”

Dow noted a recent data center failure he hopes to help prevent: a July 2026 grid disconnection in the U.S. state of Virginia that caused data centers to automatically switch to backup generators, dropping a more-than 3-gigawatt load in seconds that caused power to flicker across the eastern U.S. 

“A gigawatt is probably the power consumption of Cincinnati,” Dow said. “It’d be like Cincinnati turning all its lights on and off at every single load, simultaneously.”

SSTs are set to enter AI data centers as traditional transformers made of copper coils and magnetic iron cores struggle to meet rising demands for efficiency, power density, and scalability. Increasing rack power levels and fluctuating AI workloads cause energy losses, thermal challenges, and system complexity, power IC maker Microchip noted. SSTs directly convert medium-voltage grid power like 13.8 kV to 35 kV AC into high-voltage 800 VDC in a single step.

SSTs use wide-bandgap semiconductors such as silicon carbide (SiC) to replace conventional transformers with power electronic systems that enable intelligent control of power flow from a variety of sources including, potentially, a microgrid on the site of an AI data center.

“We can run in a microgrid,” Dow said. “We can take medium voltage off a turbine, or from the grid; we actually don’t care where it comes from, we’re like a universal power adapter.”

Supercharged

The SST segment has been “supercharged” after Nvidia, Google, and Microsoft last year announced an open-standard 800 VDC power architecture for next-generation AI data center racks, Xora Innovation chief investment officer Phil Inagaki told EE Times in an interview. Inagaki is Amperesand’s founding CEO turned board chair, who provided Xora’s venture capital to the 2023 startup as a bet on needed improvements in the AI infrastructure.

“A solid-state transformer takes AC power from the grid and can efficiently, safely convert it to DC,” Inagaki said. “It’s also bi-directional, and you can integrate battery or local generation, the grid, and your AI load. Rather than big magnets and copper wires, it is an intelligent device that can respond extremely quickly.”

The concept of solid-state transformers has been around for decades, but without the latest generation of power semiconductors, the practical implementation didn’t make sense, Inagaki noted.

Dow, a former Tesla executive, said he joined Amperesand last year to “transform the grid” by launching SSTs. 

“At Tesla, we famously in the Model 3 built a huge production line that was super automated; the alien dreadnought, as Elon [Musk] called it, but it was very difficult to scale because it was so complex,” Dow said. “I learned from that lesson. Learned how to build your product, iterate rapidly. This facility in Reno, Nevada, that I’m in is where we’re doing just that. We build our power stages, power electronics converters, the SST system. We test it on site; we have a whole validation closed loop.”

Inside the SST

The Amperesand product is a modular power converter with blocks called power stage modules, or PSMs.

“Each PSM is a standardized element that has medium-voltage to low-voltage isolation in it, and a power conversion system that samples a portion of the AC waveform from the medium-voltage side and then produces a low-voltage output that’s galvanically isolated,” Dow said.

“You can stack them in series to modularly select the amount of voltage,” he continued. “It’s a very intelligent product, so all the modules interoperate as a set. They’re synchronized all very precisely to convert the waveforms. It’s not a rectifier; it’s a bidirectional power converter. Our design is very custom-targeted to the AI factory transition that’s occurring with 800 VDC and beyond.”

The company is aiming for 98.5% efficiency at full power.

“If you think of the traditional system that would do this, you would essentially have a transformer-rectifier combo, plus you’d have a converter for a battery backup,” Dow said. “We essentially replace a UPS by adding a battery to our unit.”

According to Dow, the company has a major hyperscaler among its first customers, but he declined to name it.

“We’re also partnering to test with them at a national laboratory this year, so we’re deploying the unit to a national lab,” Dow said. Among the company’s other first customers is a traditional electrical OEM.

“It’s one of the ‘Big Five’, I’ll say,” Dow added. “Think of ABB, Eaton, Schneider, Siemens [Dow did not name the fifth company]. They’ve taken a minority investment in our company. We’ve done a very significant partnership with them for multiple hyperscalers.”

Other applications

Amperesand is evaluating more applications in photovoltaics and battery energy storage systems.

“Those are two major verticals,” Dow said. “The photovoltaic industry is huge in terms of electrical scale, at 600 gigawatts a year plus capacity. It’s a very large total addressable market, one even bigger than data centers. But it’s also got a lot of commoditization; there’s a lot of competitors worldwide.”

The company is also working with a partner on port electrification.

“One thing that’s very interesting about ships is they run medium-voltage networks,” Dow said. “They’re like a city. They come to these ports, and they run their diesel engines while they’re unloading. A ship might pull anywhere from 7 to 10 megawatts of power while at dock. We have our first customer with that. That’ll be in late 2027.”

Amperesand has been talking with a power utility in California about another product, a 10- to 20-kilovolt transformer mounted on an electrical pole that could help to prevent forest fires.

“We can actually shut off a load automatically if there’s a fault during a fire season in California,” Dow said. “You can kill a line that runs through the mountains if there’s a fire-risk day.”
